extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communications managers, and PR students (including investor-relations specialists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing, targeting, evaluating educational/economic-education programs and on objectives, legal constraints, and best practices for financial (investor) public relations. Covers audiences, topics, media, evaluation methods, and disclosure policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic objectives of educational programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating and understanding are basic objectives: a good teacher communicates, helps students retain the message, and has enough credibility so that students believe that what he or she says is factual (message acceptance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design educational-relations efforts to (1) communicate with students, teachers, employees, or other publics; (2) help publics retain the message (message retention); and (3) achieve message acceptance by establishing credibility. For school programs, ensure teachers use your materials by involving them in producing and reviewing materials for accuracy and balance and by involving antagonists to ensure classroom acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: TPF&C 'five pitfalls' of economic-education programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Towers, Perrin, Forster and Crosby study identified five 'pitfalls' in economic-education programs: lack of objectivity; 'flag-waving'; failure to meet audience needs; failure to limit subject matter; failure to consider graphic design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid propaganda or one-sided presentations; tailor content to audience needs and cognitive levels; keep subject matter focused and appropriate in scope; and attend to visual/graphic design to aid comprehension and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric focus for newer economic-education programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer programs are 'sharply focused in two critical areas': (1) winning support from key 'constituencies'—especially employees and stockholders; (2) addressing the legitimate concerns of publics considered important to the organization sponsoring the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt two-way symmetric approaches (dialogue) with key publics, especially employees and shareholders, and address their legitimate concerns rather than only promoting abstract pro-system messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and prioritize target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: TPF&C found the most frequent target publics of economic-education programs to be (in descending order): employees; the 'general' public; students; employees' families; shareholders; opinion leaders; teachers; managers; retirees; consumers; community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map program audiences explicitly, prioritize publics (employees often top), and recognize overlap with public affairs, employee relations, and environmental relations; design messages and media accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics to emphasize in economic-education programs
rubrics_metrics.description: What distinguishes economic-education programs is their emphasis on the function of the capitalist economic system and its relation to government. Frequent topics include: profits; free enterprise system; government regulation; taxation; general economic principles; productivity; inflation; competition; energy; employee benefits; capital investment; consumerism; employee compensation; job security; business cycles; environment; financial planning; world economic systems; stock market; company policies; exports; interest; retained earnings; product and service quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics that explain how the economic system operates and what business is doing to correct poor performance; include both system-level topics and concrete company consequences to improve relevance and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of methods and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic-education materials fall into categories: one-time publications (articles, annual reports, special publications or kits, curriculum or meeting leader guides) and ongoing series (articles, leaflets, posters, brochures, audiovisual materials, multimedia materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose from one-time and ongoing formats, and combine print, audiovisual, and multimedia to reach different publics and learning styles; consider case studies and kits for classroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve teachers and other stakeholders in development
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain teacher acceptance, involve teachers in producing and reviewing materials for accuracy and balance; some programs hire teachers to observe company operations and contribute firsthand perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage intended users (teachers, students) and even antagonists (environmentalists, consumerists) in development and review to improve balance, credibility, and classroom adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design programs for student relevance (situational theory application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students will only passively process educational-relations materials unless they relate to topics that involve the students. The situational theory constructs—problem recognition, level of involvement, and constraint recognition—predict whether publics will process information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select issues that directly affect target student or public groups (secondary consequences like quality, prices, pollution for journalism students), use dialogue programs to surface topics of interest, and avoid abstract, system-only propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-based mass campaigns plus supplemental materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass advertising alone cannot create knowledge. The Ad Council project used research to define realistic approaches and developed a booklet, supplementary materials, films, teaching guides, and news releases, recognizing that only a fraction of responders read booklets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to identify public knowledge gaps and attitudes; pair mass advertising to raise awareness with substantive take-away materials and educational supports; weigh costs because mass campaigns mostly reach passive publics with low retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage evaluation of educational materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational relations and economic education programs can be evaluated in three stages: (1) pretest materials experimentally with students or teachers, asking whether topics are relevant/interesting and administering retention and acceptance test questions; (2) evaluate materials for balance and fairness by asking representatives of government agencies, activist groups, or other antagonists to review and suggest changes; (3) measure communication objectives by counting the number of students or teachers who use the materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine experimental pretesting (with concrete test questions), third-party balance reviews, and usage metrics to estimate how many have been communicated with and how many retained or believed the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete test questions for message-retention and acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of evaluation questions: a multiple-choice question testing retention (e.g., 'An increase in the money supply has the effect of: (a) Raising prices and lowering the value of money...') and a belief/acceptance question (e.g., 'A fault of the business system... stockholders get too much of the money companies make... — Agree/Disagree/No opinion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clear factual and attitude/belief questions aligned to learning objectives; use results to refine content and measure program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate balance and fairness via antagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: After pretesting for retention and acceptance, evaluate materials for balance and fairness by asking representatives of government agencies, activist groups, or other antagonists to evaluate the materials and suggest what they should include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively solicit critique from credible external critics to improve objectivity and classroom acceptability; inclusion of dissenting perspectives increases perceived fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count usage to measure communication reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the communication objective by counting the number of teachers contacted and the number of students who use the company's materials; combine usage counts with retention/acceptance measures to estimate impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track distribution and uptake metrics (contacts, downloads, classroom adoptions) and triangulate with retention/acceptance test results for comprehensive evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial PR core professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The financial public relations man must be professional, have a high regard for truthfulness and accuracy, and 'lean on the side of conservatism in discussing future developments of his company.' Success reflected in a realistic appraisal of the company and its securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and conservative forward-looking statements; avoid hype and inaccurate optimism; ensure communications reflect realistic assessments to build credibility with investors and analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal constraints and disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal requirements for adequate and timely disclosure of financial information essentially limit financial PR specialists to the public-information or two-way symmetric models of public relations. 'Touting stock is illegal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with SEC and exchange disclosure rules; avoid selective disclosure, promotional touting, and any communications that could be construed as market manipulation; align investor communications with legal counsel and filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eugene Miller's common-sense disclosure policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Release immediately any news that might have a material effect on the price of the company’s securities; maintain adequate security on confidential information until it is ready; act promptly to dispel unfounded rumors causing unusual market activity; avoid premature announcements, unwarranted claims, and overly optimistic forecasts; avoid providing one inquirer with information that would not be given to another; ensure news is handled in proper perspective by avoiding over-optimism or unwarranted conservatism and by supplementing news releases when circumstances change; 'When in doubt ... DISCLOSE.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt written procedures implementing these policies; train spokespeople; treat material information uniformly and promptly; document decisions about disclosure and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication, retention, and acceptance objectives for financial publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial PR should strive to achieve the communication, message-retention, and message-acceptance objectives: communicate financial information to key publics, help those publics understand that information, and try to get those publics to believe what they are told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure investor materials not only to inform but to educate (clarify implications), and to build credibility through consistency, accuracy, and frankness; measure understanding and belief via surveys and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference Board's common financial PR objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Five objectives commonly mentioned: (1) good communications; (2) building a strong, ongoing relationship with analysts; (3) developing an informed market (message-retention); (4) establishing credibility (message-acceptance); (5) the price of the stock or the price/earnings ratio as a long-term behavior objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate PR activities into these objectives: prioritize analyst relations and two-way communication; aim to educate the market; build long-term credibility; recognize limitations of PR alone to alter stock price but work to make market valuation accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit opinions and listen to financial publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Many financial PR practitioners use interpersonal communication and surveys to solicit opinions from stockholders and analysts; however, studies show many corporations do more telling than listening—only 22% had organized programs for soliciting opinions from stockholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement structured listening programs (surveys, analyst meetings, investor panels) to learn investor needs and improve symmetric communication; measure and report back on how feedback shaped actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and simplification for nonprofessional investors
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient: it is easy to release all information with little interpretation. Message retention and acceptance require interpretation and simplification—especially for the nonprofessional small investor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide plain-language explanations, context, and interpretation of financial data (see financial writing guidance); use summaries, FAQs, and illustrative examples to aid comprehension for nonprofessional audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify four groups of financial publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial publics can usually be identified from four groups: current shareholders; prospective shareholders; the financial community (bankers, brokers, investment advisers, trustees, security analysts, and managers of mutual funds, insurance companies, and pension funds); (and others implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment investor audiences and tailor communications and channels (earnings releases, analyst briefings, investor presentations, direct mail) to each group's needs and information-seeking behavior.
